beats.detail: a task card appears at the top right: "Example task. How should we respond to a low-cost competitor?" Ten blank plans appear in two rows of five, each with a red dot, labelled "The {group}". Under a line on the card, the context appears one item at a time: its prices, our patents, dealers, price-led buyers, service revenue.

beats.text: Each asks the company's AI for an outline. They come back alike.
beats.detail: a grey box marked AI appears at the top left. A small mark travels from each red dot up to it, and ten grey outlines drop back into the plans, all in the same pattern.

beats.text: Each writes their own plan. {reviewer_sees} that each holds up.
beats.detail: each dot writes over its outline, and each plan turns to ink in its own layout: headings, bullets, a chart, a table, dense text, two columns, a numbered list, a pull quote, a timeline, a map. "AI outline, write" and "All drafted with AI" appear. A navy ring steps across the plans and leaves a tick on each.

each plan's first line is outlined, then lifts out and joins a list at the right: "How do we stand out?", "Why pay more for ours?", "Why are we worth more?", "What can't they copy?", "Where do we add value?", "Can we stay premium?", "Can we out-serve them?", "Which features win?", "Can we keep our edge?", "What earns a premium?". The plans stay where they are, ticked.

beats.text: Different words, one frame: each plan differentiates.
beats.detail: a navy reading mark appears beside each line in turn. Then a bracket closes around all ten, labelled "One frame: differentiate".

beats.text: {reviewer_doesnt_see}: almost every AI outline opened with that frame.
beats.detail: a grey card comes out of the AI box: "Almost every outline opened: Differentiate on value". A grey label above the card reads "Not seen by the manager". A grey line runs from it to the bracket, which turns grey, and settles dashed; a grey tag beside the bracket reads "AI's frame". The manager sees only the finished plans; the card and the grey are for the viewer.
beside the bracket, in open space, a dashed box appears, labelled "{reviewer_ask}", with the question inside: "What frames are missing?"

beats.text: Imagine the manager sends them back: what else could the problem be?
beats.detail: the first run moves to the upper half and dims, with the grey card above its list and the question box beside it. A navy line runs from the question box down to a heading: "Sent back: what else could the problem be?". Below a line, "Same {group}, imagined" appears with ten blank plans. Each dot writes a red first line, and its label begins "Define problem".

beats.text: Each defines the problem first, then asks the AI to challenge it.
beats.detail: a copy of each red line goes up to the AI box. A grey speech bubble appears: "What did you assume? What other frames fit?", and small grey speech bubbles land on each plan under its red line. Each dot writes its plan. The label now reads "Define problem, AI challenges, write", and the plans are marked "All drafted with AI".

beats.text: These hold up too. {reviewer_lines} them up again.
beats.detail: the speech bubble fades, the first run returns to full strength, and a navy ring ticks each imagined plan. Group by group, their problem lines lift out as words into three labelled columns under the heading: differentiate ("How do we stand out?", "Why pay more for ours?", "Why are we worth more?"); match on cost ("Can we win on cost?", "Who buys on price?", "Can we cut unit costs?", "Who is switching?"); partner or license ("Should we partner?", "License our designs?", "Supply the rival?"). Brackets close around them.

page.title: Institutional monoculture
page.description: Ten plans drafted with the same AI can each pass review and still share one definition of the problem. Lining up their problem statements shows it.
page.setup: Ten {people} at an industrial-equipment maker each use the company's AI to help answer the CEO's question: how should we respond to a low-cost competitor? Each writes their own plan, and each plan holds up when read alone. What can still go wrong is institutional monoculture: shared systems and defaults narrow the range of frames a group considers. It can happen wherever people ask the same AI, like a nonprofit's program team asking how to respond to a funder's new priority. Illustration based on Romasanta, Thomas & Levina (2026) and Bottesch (2025). The {group}, the question and the plans are constructed.

checkLines: What frames are missing across the {group}?
Line up the problems. What else could the problem be?
page.checkFollow: Read one at a time, every plan holds up. The plans differ in their details, like names, numbers and products, but lined up, they share one problem definition, the one almost every AI outline opened with. The manager never sees those outlines; the lineup of finished plans is enough to show the shared frame. Lining up shows which frames a {group} has. It can't show which are missing. For that, {reviewer_ask_l} what else the problem could be, drawing on their own knowledge of the market or on frames the {group} names before discussion settles on one. In the imagined rerun the manager sends the plans back with that question. Each analyst then writes a problem frame without AI and asks an AI to find assumptions they missed and suggest other frames, as the original essay, *The Irreducible Officer*, proposes. Whether framing first spreads frames across a {group} is untested, and the imagined board is one possible answer. Agreement can also come from a shared purpose or strong evidence, and a different frame isn't better by itself. A {group} can compare several frames and still agree on one.

about.text: Each plan's first line is its problem statement: the question the plan sets out to answer. The figure groups problems by the goal they set, and names three goals for the imagined {group} as one possible answer. Telling real frames apart takes reading. The plans, their problem lines and the AI's opening line are constructed. They don't show the output of any model or the plans of any real company.

study: Romasanta, Thomas and Levina asked leading AI models for strategic advice. Their summary of the work reports: "Across thousands of simulations, we saw LLMs almost uniformly select the same trendy strategies, regardless of context." They name the pattern: "We call the propensity for AI to opt for buzzy ideas over reasoned solutions 'trendslop.'"

That summary names no strategies, and the *Harvard Business Review* article itself, a practitioner piece, is paywalled. Coverage of the article reports that the models' defaults included differentiation over commoditization, along with augmentation over automation and the long term over the short term. The figure's AI frame, "Differentiate on value", follows that reported default. The plans and their problem lines are constructed.

Bottesch ran a field experiment with "99 knowledge workers from a multinational industrial corporation" and found "that indeed significant homogenisation effects occur in terms of style and content when knowledge workers are supported by GenAI (versus when they are not)". The abstract also offers "initial evidence that these effects might be mitigated through advanced prompting and (more) critical handling of GenAI output by knowledge workers." It is a single-author conference paper from one company, and the abstract gives no effect sizes. The figure draws the plans in different layouts so the shared frame has something to hide behind; Bottesch found that style converged as well.

Neither study lined up a team's plans or tested defining the problem first. The lineup and the imagined {group} are this figure's illustration of what the findings could mean for a team that drafts with one AI.

Counter-evidence: Terwiesch et al. (*Production and Operations Management*, 2026) found that better prompting, assigned personas and pooling several vendors brought the diversity of AI-generated ideas close to human levels. With Bottesch's mitigation finding, that suggests sameness is the default, and deliberate design can push against it.

Sources: Romasanta, Thomas & Levina, "Researchers Asked LLMs for Strategic Advice. They Got 'Trendslop' in Return," *Harvard Business Review* (March 2026), quoted from the authors' summary on NYU Stern's research highlights page; the reported defaults are from coverage of the article. Bottesch, "Towards Generative Monoculture? Insights from a Field Experiment on Style and Content Homogenisation Effects in GenAI-Supported Knowledge Work," ACIS 2025 Proceedings, quoted from the abstract. The {group}, the question, the plans and the AI's outlines are constructed. The figure shows none of either study's data.
